_description: Plex Media Server: hardware transcoding through /dev/dri, a persistent config directory and a TCP health check on 32400. Works with the official image or a slimmer community rebuild.
_comment_matches: Matches the official image and the common community rebuilds, so a pull of any of them is told this profile exists.
_comment:
A PROFILE, not a recipe - deliberately. Which image you run is a real choice (see _comment_image), your media lives wherever your disks are, and the first start needs a claim token that is valid for four minutes. A recipe would have to guess all three. This carries the part that is genuinely hard to get right instead:

  uxc pull --profile plex <image> plex

then edit the volumes in /etc/uxc/plex.json and set PLEX_CLAIM before the first start.
_comment_image:
Pick one; uxcd tracks whatever you pull and upgrades that:
  plexinc/pms-docker:latest  - official, Ubuntu-based (~400 MB). There is also a 'plexpass' tag carrying beta builds, which needs a Plex Pass account.
  spritsail/plex-media-server, forumi0721/alpine-plex - community Alpine rebuilds (~100-120 MB). Smaller, and next to a single film the difference is noise; the trade-off is a single-maintainer repack of proprietary software, so check when it was last updated before relying on it. Plex Pass FEATURES (hardware transcoding, offline sync) are tied to the signed-in account, not the image - a community build serves a Plex Pass user fine, it just tracks public releases rather than the beta channel.
_comment_caps: The entrypoints chown the config tree and drop to an unprivileged user. Listed so the profile also works with --caps minimal.
_comment_mounts: Transcoding writes large temporary files. The default tmpfs is unbounded and it is RAM - bound it, or point /transcode at a disk volume in _registry below instead.

_registry._comment_devices: The iGPU, for hardware transcoding (a Plex Pass feature). Passed through as a directory so re-enumeration keeps working, and skipped automatically on a box without one. Software transcoding needs no device at all.
_registry._comment_volumes: EDIT THESE. The config directory is the irreplaceable one: it holds the library database, watch state and metadata. Media is mounted read-only - Plex never needs to write to it, and a library scan cannot then damage the originals.
_registry._comment_env: PLEX_CLAIM links the server to your account on FIRST start and expires in four minutes - get a fresh one from https://plex.tv/claim right before starting, then remove it. ADVERTISE_IP must be the address clients actually reach, which in an infra netns is the PUBLISHED host address, not the container's.
_registry._comment_ports: Plex speaks on 32400. On the host stack it is already reachable; in an infra netns publish it - "ports": [ "32400:32400" ] - and set ADVERTISE_IP to http://<host-ip>:32400/. Note that a published port is a userspace proxy, so Plex sees the forwarder as the client: its 'allowed networks' / LAN detection will treat every client as remote. For Plex specifically an fw4 redirect is usually the better answer; see docs/networking.md.
_registry.notes: Set PLEX_CLAIM from https://plex.tv/claim (valid four minutes) before the FIRST start, then drop it. /srv/plex/config is the backup unit - the library database and watch state live there; media can be re-scanned, that cannot. Media is mounted read-only on purpose. Hardware transcoding needs /dev/dri and a Plex Pass account. In an infra netns, set ADVERTISE_IP to the published host address or clients will be handed an address they cannot reach, and remember that a published port makes every client look remote to Plex's LAN detection.
